items.prompt: What must be true of a list before a binary search can be used on it?
items.explanation: Binary search discards half the list by comparing with the middle item, which only works when the items are in order.

items.prompt: Use binary search to find 34 in the sorted list [3, 8, 15, 21, 34, 40, 57] (indexes 0 to 6).
steps: mid = (0 + 6) // 2 = 3. Item 21 is less than 34, so set low = 4.
mid = (4 + 6) // 2 = 5. Item 40 is greater than 34, so set high = 4.
mid = (4 + 4) // 2 = 4. Item 34 equals the target: found at index 4 after 3 comparisons.
Python: while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2; if a[mid] == t: return mid; elif a[mid] < t: low = mid + 1; else: high = mid - 1
Java: while (low <= high) { int mid = (low + high) / 2; if (a[mid] == t) return mid; else if (a[mid] < t) low = mid + 1; else high = mid - 1; }
items.explanation: Each comparison halves the search range, giving about log2(n) comparisons in the worst case.

items.prompt: In the worst case, how many comparisons does a linear search of n unsorted items make?
items.explanation: If the target is last or absent, every item is checked once.

items.prompt: After the first full pass of a bubble sort into ascending order, which value is guaranteed to be in its final position?
items.explanation: Adjacent swaps carry the largest value to the end of the list during the first pass.

items.answer: Repeatedly find the smallest item in the unsorted part of the list and swap it into the first unsorted position, so the sorted section grows by one item each pass.
items.explanation: It makes about n squared / 2 comparisons whatever the starting order, but at most n - 1 swaps.

items.prompt: Describe how a merge sort works.
items.answer: Split the list in half repeatedly until each part has one item, then merge pairs of sorted parts back together by repeatedly taking the smaller front item, until one sorted list remains.
